records.subagent_summary: All 8 public rollouts scored 0 (execution 149.238) and every one boxed the same wrong divisor 143, none hitting the token cap this time. The shared path: open a separate self-contained case for the sum reading and for the product reading, note inside each case that a speaker's own value plus that fixed reading determines the partner, declare that case contradictory, and then collapse to the product reading and pick the factor that merely looks special. Not one rollout pooled the partners implied by both readings into a single list for one private value, and not one allowed the two private values to be equal, so none ever saw why residual ambiguity exists. The revision makes that pooled per-value count the central operation, states that pinning under each choice taken alone is not a contradiction, and turns the word "impossible" into a trigger to redo the pooled count instead of guessing a divisor.

7 of 8 rollouts scored 1 (3.8k-5.6k tokens, 6-18 hedges). The one failure reached the modulus step at once, then nth-rooted the constant by reading it as a familiar base to a smaller exponent, inflating the ratio; it ran the incumbent coordinate route flawlessly on that wrong ratio, yielding a self-consistent circle. It then burned ~2k tokens on a false alarm: it solved the bars-drop equation on line ab, got a genuine locus point, mistook it for the center, saw a mismatch, and argued itself back into the wrong circle instead of rechecking the ratio. Correct rollouts also wasted 10-25 exponentials listing roots. Prior rounds tried symbolic k-lectures and audit rules and lost heldout, so this revision instead adds a normalization step (fold stray factors and ratio forms into c before touching moduli), where the exponent misread originates, and closes with a portable conversion menu so the locus maps to whatever a variant asks for.

Round-12 training scored 6/8. Both failures ended cleanly (finish_reason=stop, no budget loss) on the same committed error: overlap = all of S. Each argued containment purely from reach, comparing the max distance from the shared point to S's farthest corner against the big shape's half-diagonal, then set overlap = area(S) and answered areas-sum-minus-area(S). The incumbent already forbids containment verdicts and point-to-side distances, but a bare prohibition loses to a concrete-looking radius computation, and neither failure ever tested a single point of S for coverage. So this revision converts the ban into a positive, cheap obligation: in the corner-edge frame, name one point of S with a negative coordinate (uncovered) and one strictly inside the wedge (covered), which refutes containment and disjointness at once, and explicitly voids reach/diagonal/half-width arguments as evidence about which side of a line a point lies on.

My 8 rollouts scored 2/8: two wrong-answer stops and four truncations. Both wrong stops reported N (the family size): each computed a single function's successive difference as a polynomial, ruled it cannot be constant, and concluded one index per function. Two truncations chained adjacent board entries into a shift construction and never partitioned; one restated the hint then stalled; one had already reached the per-group product but looped doubting it as too high. So the live faults are the identity-vs-pointwise confusion feeding the N answer, plus doubt-loops after the bound. Rather than adding prohibitions (round 11's reject-rule variant collapsed to 3/8), this revision keeps the proven skeleton and points the existing construction device at that objection: P = T + c*prod(x-n_j) has full degree yet matches T across its whole block, so its own steps there really do equal T's difference.

records.mutation: exponentiate-separately-instead-of-log-identities, plus back-substitute the fitted parameters, and reframe no-real-root as a fit/direction bug
records.subagent_summary: 6/8 correct; both failures hit the 16384-token cap after a negative discriminant, then thrashed on diagonal-midpoint restatements (12 and 5 mentions) and on the problem being contradictory. Distinct root causes, one shared step. One combined the two curve equations via log identities using log_{1/2}2 = +1, so the argument factor came out inverted (A = B/2 instead of A = 2B) and the quadratic had no real root. The other slipped arithmetic in the parameter fit (scaled only one side by 3), got wrong parameters, never substituted them back into either given point, and ground out a four-digit-coefficient quadratic. Correct rollouts instead exponentiated each point's equation on its own and checked the fit. So the revision bans log-identity combination in favour of exponentiate-then-divide, adds a back-substitution check on the fitted parameters, and reframes no real root as a fit or direction bug instead of an inconsistent problem.

All 8 rollouts scored 0; the graded quantity is the last sub-answer, and every rollout botched it even when its earlier part used sane branch counting. Five (idx 0,1,2,4,7) declared the destination order a uniformly random permutation and read off 1/4; four of those also defined the destination bottom as the LAST item moved, inverting the pile, which makes the asked position untestable. Two (idx 5,6) stayed probabilistic but priced the event with a single lone 1/2, as if only one step mattered. So the live defects are the orientation flip and undercounting how many genuine choices the event forces. This revision keeps the incumbent's near-minimal length and its 1/2-per-free-step pricing, adding only bottom=first arrival and the fact that delivering a buried item first needs a run of consecutive same-direction moves, each a separate choice. Rounds 1-11 show every rewrite past ~130 tokens lost held-out, so this stays at 122.

3/8 correct; all three winners just solved n=2,3,4 numerically and fit the pattern. The dominant waste in the five failures is not the fit but the setup: four spent 1500+ tokens circularly re-arguing how many conditions a toy with n unknowns should carry, oscillating between n and n+1, then declared the resulting over-determined toy inconsistent and abandoned the ladder for symbolic Vandermonde/elementary-symmetric/harmonic-sum work (two hit the cap mid-loop, one degenerated into literal token repetition). Two carried unverified toy values (denominators 19 and 791) forward. One built no toy at all, guessed the family from a theorem name, and got the sign and offset wrong. So this revision makes the scaling rule a one-time count-matching commitment that must not be renegotiated, forces per-case back-substitution, and derives growth plus sign from consecutive ratios.

All 8 rollouts scored reward 1 (train_i=1.0), so headroom is transfer only (incumbent heldout 12/80). The rollouts derive the divisor set fast, then burn hundreds of tokens asking WHY the maximum common divisor is intended, quoting the hint's 'maximum feasible count' clause back as bare authority (7-22 'wait' backtracks, up to 6.7k tokens). Prior rounds show what happens when that reason is absent: r10/r11 rollouts reached the same divisor list, then picked the small candidate 'because the problem is likely designed to have a unique answer' and landed on the wrong scale. Restating the rule harder (r5, r6, r9, r11) did not help. So I keep the kept-hint spine (gcd, groups x units-per-group) and supply the missing justification: smaller divisors also divide evenly, so divisibility cannot select them, and a stated integrality condition is informative only if it pins one value. I also add a check-if-N-is-given branch so the gcd machinery is not forced onto problems that state the count.

7 of 8 rollouts correct (3.1k-6.6k tokens). The single failure burned the full 16384-token cap: composing the centered maps it re-cubed an already-cubed offset, getting BA^9 instead of BA^3, hence B^2=A^8 and B=+-A^4 (70 A^4 mentions). It then chased that corrupted branch, declared the system underdetermined, and only stumbled onto a consistent center by integer guessing at the very end, too late to finish. Three correct rollouts briefly flirted with the same A^4 slip, and 'another fixed point' hunts appear in 5 of 8 tails. Rounds 9 and 10 already tried exponent-audit wording and both lost heldout, so instead this revision lifts the round-7 add/subtract rule from numeric conditions to the unknown functions themselves: p+q constant on the sign-flipped branch pins the center as an average, converts any known value of one map into the other, and shows the center is forced so the fixed-point hunt ends.

2/8 correct with the incumbent; all six failures ran to the 16384-token cap. Four collapsed each block swap into a single transposition, declared the composite a product of disjoint 2-cycles, and concluded order 2 -- one even wrote cycle products on non-overlapping index sets -- without ever writing the state after two full repeats to check. The rest thrashed between mutually inconsistent per-size counts (one asserted 12 for a size, then invented piecewise formulas depending on n) and never committed. Nobody tested minimality, so nothing caught the too-small count. The revision keeps the incumbent's state-rewriting and single-convention mechanisms but adds the quantitative reason the order-2 story is wrong (a length-L block swap is L parallel swaps moving 2L slots, and nested ranges cannot be disjoint) plus an explicit proper-divisor minimality check that forces any small candidate to be exhibited rather than assumed.
